patient.name: Funmilayo Adeyemi
patient.complaint: Severe epigastric pain going through to her back, with vomiting, for 8 hours
background: Two episodes of right upper quadrant pain after meals last year
Drinks 4 units of alcohol a week
Lives in Lewisham with her husband

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting and a raised amylase, in a stem that hides gallstones or alcohol as the cause.

points: Funmilayo, 58, woke at 2 am with **severe epigastric pain**.
The pain **bores through to her back**.
Sitting forward eases it a little; lying flat is worse.
She has vomited six times and feels sweaty.

steps.lead: Pain like Funmilayo's comes from enzymes switching on **inside** the pancreas and digesting it. Her past post-meal RUQ pain hints at **gallstones**.

visual.title: Where Funmilayo's pain is
visual.caption: Epigastric pain radiating to the back, eased by leaning forward: the pancreas sits in the retroperitoneum behind the stomach.

steps.lead: Funmilayo has the full picture: epigastric pain to the back, vomiting, tenderness and early **tachycardia**.
Funmilayo drinks little, takes no valproate and has not had an ERCP: her likely cause is **gallstones**.

steps.q: Her amylase comes back at 1,860 U/L (<220). What is the most likely cause in Funmilayo?
steps.r: Previous post-prandial RUQ pain in an overweight woman with low alcohol intake points to **gallstones**, the commonest cause.

steps.title: Epigastric pain to the back: what else?
head: Feature
Acute pancreatitis
Perforated peptic ulcer
Ruptured AAA
rows: Epigastric to back, eased leaning forward

steps.text: A mildly raised amylase (e.g. 258 U/L) does **not** make it pancreatitis. Perforated ulcer, cholecystitis and bowel ischaemia nudge amylase up; you need **3x the upper limit**.

steps.lead: Funmilayo's SpO2 of 95% and tachycardia are warnings: severe disease can bring **effusions, ARDS, necrosis** and later a **pseudocyst**.

steps.text: Pain plus **persistently raised amylase about 4 weeks** after an attack, with an epigastric fullness, is a **pseudocyst** until proven otherwise.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (serum amylase or lipase), then ultrasound for the cause, CT only if unsure or complications, and the Glasgow-Imrie score at 48 hours.

steps.title: Funmilayo's bloods on arrival
steps.text: Amylase over 8x the upper limit of normal. The raised ALT points to a gallstone cause.

steps.lead: Funmilayo's typical pain plus an amylase far above **3x the upper limit** confirms acute pancreatitis. No scan is needed to make the diagnosis.

visual.title: Serum amylase (U/L)
visual.label: Funmilayo 1,860
visual.caption: The diagnostic cut-off is 3x the upper limit (here 660 U/L). Amylase height does not predict severity.

steps.q: Diagnosis confirmed. Which imaging should Funmilayo have next?
steps.r: **Ultrasound** looks for gallstones as the cause. CT is for diagnostic doubt or suspected complications.

steps.lead: Funmilayo's ultrasound shows **multiple gallstones** and a common bile duct of 6 mm: a gallstone cause.
Funmilayo does not need CT now. If she failed to improve, a **CT abdomen** after a few days would look for necrosis or collections.
Score Funmilayo with **PANCREAS**: PaO2, Age, WBC, Calcium, Albumin and Sugar are all positive. Urea and LDH miss their cut-offs.

visual.title: Modified Glasgow (Imrie) score at 48 h
visual.label: Funmilayo 6
visual.caption: A score of 3 or more is severe pancreatitis with a poor prognosis: think HDU/ICU.

steps.text: The Glasgow score is calculated at **48 hours**, not at triage, and **amylase is not one of the criteria**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (IV crystalloid, analgesia, oxygen), plus 'next step' questions on ICU for Glasgow ≥3, no routine antibiotics, and cholecystectomy for gallstone cases.

steps.q: Funmilayo is tachycardic at 112 bpm and in severe pain. What comes first?
o: Nil by mouth and wait for CT
steps.r: **Fluid resuscitation** starts before imaging, with opioid analgesia and oxygen if hypoxic. Antibiotics are not routine.

steps.lead: Funmilayo gets **500 ml crystalloid stat** with review, IV morphine, oxygen for her SpO2 of 95%, and food as soon as she can tolerate it.

steps.title: Acute pancreatitis: first 48 hours
nodes: IV crystalloid, opioid analgesia, O2 if hypoxic
Treat the cause: ERCP if obstruction, cholecystectomy later
steps.caption: Resuscitate first, find the cause, then score the severity.

visual.title: Funmilayo's response to fluids
visual.caption: Early improvement, then deterioration by 48 h as the inflammatory response and capillary leak take hold.

steps.lead: With a Glasgow score of 6 and a PaO2 of 7.6 kPa, Funmilayo is **severe**: she is moved to **HDU/ICU** for organ support.

steps.text: Do not give prophylactic antibiotics because she has a fever or high WCC. Fever is the inflammation. Antibiotics are for **infected necrosis, cholangitis** or a confirmed infection.

steps.lead: Funmilayo's bilirubin stays normal-ish, so no ERCP. Once she recovers, she needs a **cholecystectomy** to stop it happening again.
Funmilayo's severity was scored with **Glasgow-Imrie**; Ranson and BISAP are alternative scores you may meet in stems.

steps.text: Gallstone pancreatitis + **jaundice and fever (cholangitis)** or a persistently obstructed duct = **urgent ERCP**. Otherwise, cholecystectomy after recovery.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why trypsin activation causes autodigestion, why gallstones or alcohol trigger it, why calcium falls, and why severe cases develop ARDS or third-space losses.

steps.lead: In Funmilayo, **trypsinogen** turned into **trypsin** inside the pancreas instead of in the duodenum, and trypsin switched on everything else.

steps.title: From a stone to systemic illness
nodes: Gallstone impacts at the ampulla of Vater
Raised duct pressure, reflux of bile and secretions

steps.lead: Funmilayo's stone blocked the **ampulla of Vater**. In a heavy drinker, alcohol injures **acinar cells** and forms **protein plugs** instead.
Funmilayo's falling urine output and PaO2 of 7.6 kPa are **capillary leak**: fluid moves into the gut, pleura and lungs.

visual.title: Funmilayo's chest X-ray on day 3
visual.caption: Bilateral ground-glass shadowing (ARDS) and a left pleural effusion from capillary leak.

steps.lead: Funmilayo's calcium of 1.94 mmol/L is **saponification**: free fatty acids from fat necrosis bind calcium.

steps.r: **Saponification**: fatty acids released by lipase combine with calcium in necrotic peripancreatic fat.

steps.lead: If Funmilayo returns at about **4 weeks** with fullness and a high amylase, a walled-off collection without epithelium, a **pseudocyst**, is the cause.

steps.title: Necrosis vs pseudocyst
head: Feature
Pancreatic necrosis
Pseudocyst
rows: Fluid walled off by fibrous/granulation tissue, no epithelium
Pain, bloating, pressure on nearby structures

mcq.q: What are the two most common causes of acute pancreatitis?
Which drug is a recognised cause of acute pancreatitis?
mcq.r: **Sodium valproate**, sulfonamides (co-trimoxazole), sulfasalazine and mesalazine are in the notes.

mcq.q: When does a pancreatic pseudocyst typically develop?
mcq.r: Pseudocysts form about **4 weeks** after; necrosis develops in the first week.

mcq.q: What amylase level supports a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?
mcq.r: Amylase or lipase **3x the upper limit of normal** with a typical clinical picture.

mcq.q: Why may lipase be preferred over amylase?
o: More specific and stays raised longer
mcq.r: **Lipase** is more specific and remains elevated longer.

mcq.q: When is the Modified Glasgow (Imrie) score calculated?
mcq.r: It is calculated at **48 hours**; ≥3 is severe.

mcq.q: What is the first step in managing acute pancreatitis?
mcq.r: **Crystalloid** is started before imaging, with analgesia and oxygen if hypoxic.

mcq.q: When are antibiotics indicated in acute pancreatitis?
mcq.r: Not routine: only **infected necrosis, cholangitis** or confirmed infection.

mcq.q: Which enzyme's premature activation starts acute pancreatitis?
mcq.r: **Trypsinogen to trypsin** inside the pancreas, which activates the other proenzymes.

mcq.q: Why does hypocalcaemia occur in severe pancreatitis?
mcq.r: **Saponification**: fatty acids bind calcium in necrotic fat.

technique.stem: A 47 year old man has a 12 hour history of severe epigastric pain radiating to his back and repeated vomiting. He drinks 70 units of alcohol per week. He is sitting forward on the trolley. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. His epigastrium is tender with reduced bowel sounds. His erect chest X-ray is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about epigastric pain: decide what the pain pattern and the amylase tell you.

clues: epigastric pain radiating to his back
steps.x: Classic pain, a classic cause, the classic posture, no free air, and amylase over **3x the upper limit**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Alcohol excess + epigastric pain to the back + amylase ≥3x ULN: **acute pancreatitis**.

elim: Cholecystitis is RUQ pain with Murphy's sign, and does not push amylase this high.
Alcoholic hepatitis gives jaundice and tender hepatomegaly, with AST:ALT above 2.
Perforation gives peritonism and free air; the erect CXR is normal.
Ruptured AAA gives shock and a pulsatile mass, not this amylase.

steps.x: **B. Acute pancreatitis.** Rule: typical pain + amylase or lipase ≥3x ULN = diagnosis, no scan needed.

technique.stem: A 63 year old woman has a 6 hour history of epigastric pain radiating to her back and vomiting. She drinks no alcohol and had right upper quadrant pain after meals last year. Her pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. Her serum amylase is 1,520 U/L (<220).
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to find the cause?

steps.x: The diagnosis is made; the question asks how to find the **cause**.

clues: right upper quadrant pain after meals last year
steps.x: No alcohol, past biliary colic, raised ALT: the cause is probably **gallstones**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Early **ultrasound** to look for gallstones.

elim: An X-ray misses most gallstones and adds nothing here.
CT is for diagnostic doubt or suspected complications, not the first look for stones.
ERCP is treatment for obstruction or cholangitis, not a first test.
Triglycerides are worth checking if no stones, but gallstones are far more likely here.

steps.x: **A. Abdominal ultrasound.** Amylase diagnoses it; ultrasound finds the gallstone cause.

technique.stem: A 55 year old man with alcohol excess has acute pancreatitis confirmed on admission. At 48 hours his temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. He is receiving IV fluids and morphine.
technique.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

steps.x: A next-step question at 48 hours: score severity first.
PaO2 <8, WBC >15, calcium <2, urea >16: **Glasgow 4**, plus shock and hypoxia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Glasgow ≥3 with organ failure: **HDU/ICU** for supportive care.

elim: He is shocked and hypoxic; discharge is unsafe.
A ward is not enough for a severe score with organ failure.
Antibiotics are not routine; fever here is inflammation, not proven infection.
Surgery is not the treatment for acute pancreatitis itself.

steps.x: **D. Transfer to HDU/ICU.** Glasgow-Imrie ≥3, shock, hypoxia or organ failure all mean escalate.

technique.stem: A 49 year old woman is in hospital with severe gallstone pancreatitis. On day 2 she has perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 108/70 mmHg. She has not had any thyroid or neck surgery.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hypocalcaemia?

steps.x: A mechanism question: explain the low calcium in pancreatitis.

clues: not had any thyroid or neck surgery
steps.x: True hypocalcaemia (adjusted), in severe pancreatitis, with no surgical cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fat necrosis releases fatty acids that bind calcium: **saponification**.

elim: Nephrocalcinosis is a cause of high, not low, calcium states.
No neck surgery; PTH failure is not the mechanism in pancreatitis.
Vomit contains little calcium; vomiting causes alkalosis and low potassium.
Vitamin D deficiency develops over months, not on day 2.

steps.x: **D. Saponification.** Calcium <2 mmol/L is also a Glasgow-Imrie criterion.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman has an 8 hour history of severe epigastric pain radiating through to her back, eased by leaning forward. She has vomited repeatedly. She has had previous episodes of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. Her epigastrium is tender.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Epigastric pain to the back eased by leaning forward with amylase over 3x normal is acute pancreatitis, here from gallstones. Cholangitis needs fever, jaundice and RUQ pain.

steps.x: Diagnosis: match the pain and the amylase.

clues: right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals
steps.x: Classic pancreatic pain, past biliary colic, amylase about 9x ULN.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Gallstone acute pancreatitis.**

elim: Cholangitis needs Charcot's triad; bilirubin is barely raised and no high fever.
Biliary colic has normal bloods and RUQ pain.
MI is possible in epigastric pain, but the amylase explains this picture.
Perforation gives peritonism and only a mild amylase rise.

steps.x: **B. Acute pancreatitis.** Amylase ≥3x ULN plus typical pain is enough.

practice.stem: A 39 year old man with epilepsy has a 1 day history of epigastric pain radiating to his back and vomiting. He drinks 6 units of alcohol per week. His medication was changed recently. Ultrasound shows a normal gallbladder with no stones. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 130/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his presentation?
practice.e: With no gallstones, little alcohol, normal triglycerides and calcium, a recent medication change in epilepsy points to sodium valproate-induced pancreatitis.

steps.x: It asks for the **cause** of pancreatitis: go through the list and cross off what the stem excludes.
Common causes are excluded; a new antiepileptic is the clue.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Drug-induced: **sodium valproate**.

elim: 6 units a week is not alcohol excess.
Ultrasound shows no stones.
Calcium is normal.
Triglycerides are normal.

steps.x: **E. Sodium valproate.** No stones and no alcohol: look for a drug.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man was admitted 4 weeks ago with alcohol-related acute pancreatitis. He now has dull epigastric pain, bloating, early fullness and indigestion. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. There is a vague epigastric mass.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Persistently raised amylase, bloating, dull pain and a mass about 4 weeks after an attack is a pseudocyst. Necrosis develops in the first week.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a complication: the timing is the key.

clues: dull epigastric pain, bloating, early fullness and indigestion
steps.x: Four weeks out, persistent amylase, mass effect symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pancreatic pseudocyst.**

elim: No ulcer history and vomiting is not described; the timing points to the pancreas.
Cancer presents with painless jaundice and weight loss, not 4 weeks after pancreatitis.
Necrosis develops within the first week.
A new attack gives severe acute pain, not dull bloating.

steps.x: **D. Pancreatic pseudocyst.** About 4 weeks + persistently high amylase + mass.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman is on day 3 of admission with severe gallstone pancreatitis. She becomes increasingly breathless. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86% on 40% oxygen. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray, day 3
visual.caption: Bilateral ground-glass opacities with a normal heart size.

practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her deterioration?
practice.e: Severe pancreatitis causes capillary leak and ARDS: bilateral ground-glass opacities, severe hypoxia and a normal BNP. Heart failure would give a raised BNP and cardiomegaly.

steps.x: A complication question: what explains the X-ray?
Severe disease, early, refractory hypoxia, bilateral shadowing, normal BNP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **ARDS** from pulmonary capillary leak.

elim: Aspiration gives one-sided (usually right lower) consolidation.
Normal BNP and heart size argue against heart failure.
A pneumothorax would show a visible lung edge, not bilateral shadowing.
PE usually gives a clear chest X-ray.

steps.x: **A. ARDS.** Bilateral ground glass in severe pancreatitis = capillary leak.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man had an ERCP with sphincterotomy for a common bile duct stone 6 hours ago. He now has severe epigastric pain radiating to his back and has vomited twice. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. His abdomen is soft with epigastric tenderness.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Pancreatitis is the most common complication of ERCP: epigastric pain to the back with amylase above 3x normal. Perforation gives peritonism and free gas.

steps.x: Diagnosis after a procedure: think of its commonest complication.
Recent ERCP, pancreatic pain, soft abdomen, amylase about 6x ULN.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Post-ERCP pancreatitis.**

elim: Cholangitis needs fever and jaundice.
Bile leak follows cholecystectomy, with bile in a drain.
Perforation causes peritonism; his abdomen is soft.
A retained stone causes jaundice and raised bilirubin, not this amylase.

steps.x: **D. Post-ERCP pancreatitis.** The most common complication of ERCP.

practice.stem: A 57 year old man has acute pancreatitis from alcohol. Bloods are taken 48 hours after admission. His pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely severity using the Modified Glasgow (Imrie) criteria?
practice.e: Age >55, WBC >15 and urea >16 score 3, which is severe. PaO2, calcium, albumin, glucose and LDH all miss their cut-offs.

steps.x: Severity question: run through PANCREAS against each cut-off.
Age >55 ✓, WBC >15 ✓, urea >16 ✓. PaO2 ≥8, Ca ≥2, albumin ≥32, glucose ≤10, LDH ≤600.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Score **3 = severe**.

elim: Undercounts: three criteria are met.
Undercounts by one.
Counts values that are abnormal but above the Glasgow cut-offs.
Scores every abnormal result rather than each cut-off.

steps.x: **C. Severe, score 3.** Use the cut-offs, not the reference ranges.

practice.stem: A 36 year old man has a 10 hour history of severe epigastric pain radiating to his back and vomiting after a weekend of heavy drinking. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. His epigastrium is tender with reduced bowel sounds.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
practice.e: Acute pancreatitis is confirmed by amylase or lipase at least 3x the upper limit with typical pain. CT is only for uncertainty or complications.

steps.x: Initial investigation to **confirm** the diagnosis.

clues: epigastric pain radiating to his back
steps.x: Classic alcohol-related acute pancreatitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A blood test: **amylase or lipase**.

elim: An X-ray does not diagnose pancreatitis.
CT is second-line: uncertain diagnosis or complications.
EUS is for pancreatic masses and small stones, not first-line.
MRCP images the ducts, used later for stones.

steps.x: **E. Serum lipase.** Lipase is more specific and stays raised longer than amylase.

practice.stem: A 50 year old woman was admitted 7 days ago with acute pancreatitis. She initially improved but now has a swinging fever and worsening abdominal pain. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: Deterioration a week in suggests infected pancreatic necrosis. CT abdomen is the test when complications are suspected; repeat amylase does not track severity.

steps.x: An investigation for a deteriorating patient: suspect a complication.
First week, new sepsis: **infected necrosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT abdomen** to look for necrosis or collections.

elim: Ultrasound finds gallstones but sees the pancreas poorly through gas.
An X-ray cannot show necrosis.
Amylase does not reflect severity or complications.
Endoscopy does not image the pancreas.

steps.x: **C. Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen.** CT for doubt or complications.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has severe epigastric pain radiating to her back. Her amylase is 1,700 U/L (<220). Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV crystalloid, opioid analgesia and oxygen
Nil by mouth and nasogastric tube
practice.e: Fluid resuscitation with crystalloid, opioid analgesia and oxygen for hypoxia come first, before any imaging. Antibiotics are not routine.

steps.x: Initial management: resuscitate.
Confirmed pancreatitis, hypovolaemic and hypoxic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV crystalloid, opioid and oxygen.**

elim: Antibiotics are not routine without proven infection.
Early oral feeding is encouraged; NG tube is not first.
CT is not needed to diagnose and does not come before fluids.
ERCP is for cholangitis or obstruction; neither is described.

steps.x: **B.** Fluids start even before imaging.

practice.stem: A 48 year old woman has recovered from mild acute pancreatitis. Ultrasound showed multiple gallstones with a normal calibre common bile duct. Her pain has settled and she is eating. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Gallstone pancreatitis needs cholecystectomy after recovery to prevent recurrence. ERCP is for an obstructed duct or cholangitis, which she does not have.

steps.x: Definitive management: treat the cause.
Gallstone cause, no duct obstruction, now well.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cholecystectomy** after recovery.

elim: No duct stone or cholangitis; ERCP is not needed.
Dissolution therapy is not the standard.
Diet alone leaves a high recurrence risk.
Waiting risks another attack.

steps.x: **A. Cholecystectomy.** Gallstone pancreatitis: remove the gallbladder.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has gallstone pancreatitis. On day 2 he becomes jaundiced with rigors. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct of 11 mm.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: Gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis and an obstructed duct needs antibiotics and urgent ERCP. Cholangitis is one of the few indications for antibiotics in pancreatitis.

steps.x: Next step: what has changed?

clues: dilated common bile duct of 11 mm
steps.x: Charcot's triad with an obstructed duct: **cholangitis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV antibiotics + urgent ERCP.**

elim: Cholecystectomy is later; the duct must be cleared now.
He is septic; discharge is unsafe.
No pseudocyst on day 2.
Waiting delays source control in sepsis.

steps.x: **B.** ERCP for obstruction or cholangitis.

practice.stem: A 42 year old woman has acute gallstone pancreatitis. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Her amylase is 1,600 U/L (<220). A student asks why a stone stuck at the ampulla damages the pancreas.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of pancreatic injury?
o: Bacterial infection ascending the pancreatic duct
Direct toxic injury to acinar cells
Premature activation of trypsinogen within the pancreas
practice.e: Obstruction at the ampulla raises duct pressure, and trypsinogen is activated to trypsin inside the pancreas, triggering autodigestion. Direct acinar toxicity is the alcohol mechanism.

steps.x: A mechanism question for gallstone pancreatitis.
Obstruction, reflux, raised intraductal pressure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Trypsinogen activated to trypsin** in the pancreas, not the duodenum.

elim: Autoimmune pancreatitis is a different, IgG4-related disease.
Acute pancreatitis is sterile inflammation at first.
Direct acinar toxicity is how **alcohol** causes it.
Splenic vein thrombosis is a complication, not the cause.

steps.x: **E.** The final common step for every cause is intrapancreatic trypsin activation.

prompts.q: What is acute pancreatitis, and what are its causes and risk factors?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem hides the cause; name gallstones and alcohol first.

points.p: Acute inflammation from premature activation of pancreatic enzymes (autodigestion)
points.why: The enzymes digest the pancreas itself.

points.p: Gallstones (most common cause)
points.why: Look for past biliary colic or raised ALT.

points.p: Alcohol excess
Hypertriglyceridaemia and post-ERCP
points.why: Pancreatitis is the most common complication of ERCP.

points.p: Drugs: sodium valproate, sulfonamides (co-trimoxazole), sulfasalazine, mesalazine
points.why: No stones, no alcohol: check the drug list.

prompts.q: Describe the classic presentation and examination findings of acute pancreatitis.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: where is the pain, where does it go, and what eases it?

points.p: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back
Relieved by leaning forward
Nausea and vomiting, distension, sweating
Epigastric tenderness and reduced bowel sounds
Severe: tachycardia, hypotension

prompts.q: What are the complications of acute pancreatitis, and when does each appear?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the timing in the stem tells you which complication.

points.p: Pleural effusions and third-space fluid loss
ARDS: bilateral ground-glass opacities on CXR
points.why: Severe disease, usually in the first days.

points.p: Pancreatic necrosis in the first week
Pseudocyst at about 4 weeks: persistently raised amylase, bloating, dull pain

prompts.q: How do you tell acute pancreatitis from perforated ulcer and biliary colic in a stem?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: mildly raised amylase occurs in other conditions; the 3x rule decides.

points.p: Pancreatitis: amylase or lipase at least 3x upper limit
points.why: A small rise (e.g. 258) is not diagnostic.

points.p: Perforated ulcer: peritonism and free air on erect CXR
points.why: A normal erect CXR in the stem points away from it.

points.p: Biliary colic: RUQ pain, normal bloods

prompts.q: How is acute pancreatitis diagnosed, and what imaging follows?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: blood test diagnoses, ultrasound finds the cause, CT for doubt.

points.p: Serum amylase (or lipase) at least 3x the upper limit of normal
Lipase is more specific and stays raised longer
Ultrasound to look for gallstones
points.why: Finds the cause, not the diagnosis.

points.p: CT abdomen if diagnosis uncertain or complications suspected

prompts.q: Which score assesses severity, when is it done, and what are its criteria and cut-offs?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: say PANCREAS with each number, then the 48-hour rule.

points.p: Modified Glasgow (Imrie) criteria at 48 hours
PaO2 <8 kPa, Age >55, WBC >15
Calcium <2, Urea >16
Enzymes (LDH >600 or AST/ALT >200), Albumin <32, Sugar >10
points.why: Amylase is NOT in the score.

points.p: 0–1 mild, 2 moderate, 3 or more severe

prompts.q: What is the initial management of acute pancreatitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fluids before scans; feed early.

points.p: IV crystalloid resuscitation (Hartmann's/Ringer's or 0.9% saline), started before imaging
Opioid analgesia
Oxygen if hypoxic
Early oral feeding within 24 hours; enteral nutrition if moderate or severe
points.why: Prolonged nil by mouth is outdated.

prompts.q: When do you escalate, give antibiotics, do ERCP or remove the gallbladder?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each intervention has one specific trigger.

points.p: Glasgow ≥3, shock, hypoxia, organ failure or sepsis: HDU/ICU
Antibiotics only for infected necrosis, cholangitis or confirmed infection
ERCP for obstruction or cholangitis
Cholecystectomy after recovery if gallstone-related

prompts.q: What is the pathophysiology, and how do gallstones and alcohol each cause it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one common step, two different triggers.

points.p: Premature activation of trypsinogen to trypsin inside the pancreas
Trypsin activates other proenzymes: autodigestion and systemic inflammation
Gallstones obstruct the ampulla of Vater: reflux and raised duct pressure
Alcohol: direct acinar cell toxicity and protein plugs in ducts
points.why: Direct toxicity is the alcohol answer.

prompts.q: Why does severe pancreatitis cause hypocalcaemia, third-space loss, ARDS and pseudocysts?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: link each finding to one mechanism.

points.p: Hypocalcaemia: saponification, fat necrosis binds calcium
Capillary leak syndrome from systemic inflammation

glossary.acute pancreatitis: Sudden inflammation of the pancreas caused by its own enzymes being switched on too early.
glossary.autodigestion: The pancreas being digested by its own activated enzymes.
glossary.trypsinogen: The inactive form of trypsin, normally activated only in the duodenum.
glossary.trypsin: A protein-digesting enzyme that activates the other pancreatic enzymes.
glossary.amylase: A pancreatic enzyme that digests starch; 3x the upper limit supports pancreatitis.
glossary.lipase: A pancreatic enzyme that digests fat; more specific than amylase and stays raised longer.
glossary.ULN: Upper limit of normal for a lab test.
glossary.ERCP: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography: a camera via the duodenum to image and clear bile and pancreatic ducts.
glossary.sphincterotomy: Cutting the sphincter of Oddi during ERCP to let stones pass.
glossary.ampulla of Vater: Where the common bile duct and pancreatic duct open into the duodenum.
glossary.acinar cells: The pancreatic cells that make digestive enzymes.
glossary.hypertriglyceridaemia: Very high blood triglycerides; a recognised cause of pancreatitis.
glossary.sodium valproate: An antiepileptic drug that can cause acute pancreatitis.
glossary.co-trimoxazole: A sulfonamide-containing antibiotic linked to pancreatitis.
glossary.sulfasalazine: An anti-inflammatory used in IBD and arthritis; can cause pancreatitis.
glossary.mesalazine: A 5-ASA drug for ulcerative colitis; a recognised cause of pancreatitis.
glossary.Glasgow-Imrie: The Modified Glasgow severity score for pancreatitis, done at 48 hours; 3 or more is severe.
glossary.Modified Glasgow: Severity score for acute pancreatitis using the PANCREAS criteria at 48 hours.
glossary.PANCREAS: Mnemonic: PaO2, Age, Neutrophils, Calcium, Raised urea, Enzymes, Albumin, Sugar.
glossary.Ranson's criteria: An older pancreatitis severity score using admission and 48-hour values.
glossary.BISAP: A bedside pancreatitis severity score: BUN, Impaired mental state, SIRS, Age, Pleural effusion.
glossary.LDH: Lactate dehydrogenase, an enzyme released by damaged cells; a Glasgow criterion if above 600.
glossary.PaO2: Partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood, measured on an arterial gas.
glossary.pseudocyst: A walled-off fluid collection with no epithelial lining, forming about 4 weeks after pancreatitis.
glossary.pancreatic necrosis: Dead, non-viable pancreatic tissue, developing in the first week of severe disease.
glossary.infected necrosis: Dead pancreatic tissue that has become infected; an indication for antibiotics and drainage.
glossary.debridement: Surgical or endoscopic removal of dead tissue.
glossary.ARDS: Acute respiratory distress syndrome: leaky lung capillaries causing severe hypoxia and bilateral shadowing.
glossary.ground-glass: Hazy lung shadowing on imaging through which vessels are still visible.
glossary.capillary leak: Inflamed capillaries letting fluid escape into tissues and body spaces.
glossary.third space: Fluid lost into body cavities or tissues (gut, pleura, peritoneum) rather than the circulation.
glossary.saponification: Fatty acids from fat necrosis combining with calcium, lowering serum calcium.
glossary.fat necrosis: Death of fat tissue as lipase digests it, releasing fatty acids.
glossary.SIRS: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome: whole-body inflammation with fever, tachycardia and raised WCC.
glossary.crystalloid: Clear IV fluid such as Hartmann's, Ringer's lactate or 0.9% saline.
glossary.Ringer's lactate: A balanced crystalloid fluid, very similar to Hartmann's solution.
glossary.enteral nutrition: Feeding into the gut, by mouth or tube, rather than into a vein.
glossary.cholangitis: Infection of the bile ducts, usually from a blocked duct; fever, jaundice and RUQ pain.
glossary.HDU: High dependency unit: a step between the ward and ICU.
glossary.Charcot's triad: Fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain: the signs of ascending cholangitis.
